britannica-1911-felanitx:
Felanitx, or Felaniche, is a town of Spain in the south-east of the island of Majorca in the Balearic Islands, about five miles inland from its harbour, Puerto Colon. Its population in 1900 was 11,294. Low hills stand between the town and the Mediterranean. On one summit, the Puig de San Sebastian, a Moorish castle stands, noted for a remarkable series of underground vaults cut below it.

Pottery has been made at Felanitx since the third century before Christ, and perhaps longer. Its earthenware water-coolers and other vessels are prized for beauty of form and the antiquity of their designs. Trade in the town is thriving, covering wine, fruit, wheat, cattle, brandy, chalk and soap. The short entry thus joins an old craft, a castle with vaulted chambers, and the everyday commerce of a Majorcan inland town.
doe-osti-2574798-chromatic-transport-mod:
A Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory note by Chad Mitchell, dated August 4, 2025, sets out the transport models inside ImpactX, a symplectic code for beam dynamics. Symplectic models respect the geometry of Hamiltonian motion, so simulated beams do not gain or lose energy spuriously over long runs. For straight-axis elements, the code offers three levels of approximation, and the note's focus is the middle one.

The levels run from a purely linear model, through a paraxial, or chromatic, expansion of the Hamiltonian, up to the exact nonlinear form. Expanding around the design orbit and keeping second-degree terms yields the familiar six-by-six transport matrix for linearized motion. The chromatic model keeps more physics, expanding in the transverse momenta while tracking how off-momentum particles drift. Mitchell writes the Hamiltonians explicitly in the code's six-dimensional phase space, in both dynamic and static unit systems.
doe-osti-3391132-purpose-design-and-anal:
Purpose, Design, and Analysis of the NSTX-U Centerstack Casing Lateral Support Shims is a fusion engineering paper by P. Titus, S. Gerhardt, A. Brooks, J. Fang, F. Cai, B. Meiner, and J. Wisniewski. The casing surrounds the central magnet core of the National Spherical Torus Experiment Upgrade. It forms the inner vacuum boundary of the plasma chamber. It carries the inboard plasma-facing components.

The casing stands like a cantilever, fixed at its lower flange and flexibly supported at the top by bellows. Insulated shims at the upper support react the largest share of disruption loads. Those are the violent forces a plasma collapse throws at the vessel, including the less predictable halo currents. The team also converted the shims into load cells. The supports therefore double as instruments measuring symmetric and asymmetric loading. That guides planning for runs beyond the next campaign, expected in late 2026 or early 2027.
